title: EDUCATING PSYCHE
bodyParagraphs: Educating Psyche by Bernie Neville is a book which looks at radical new approaches to learning, describing the effects of emotion, imagination and the unconscious on learning. One theory discussed in the book is that proposed by George Lozanov, which focuses on the power of suggestion.

Lozanov’s instructional technique is based on the evidence that the connections made in the brain through unconscious processing (which he calls non-specific mental reactivity) are more durable than those made through conscious processing. Besides the laboratory evidence for this, we know from our experience that we often remember what we have perceived peripherally, long after we have forgotten what we set out to learn. If we think of a book we studied months or years ago, we will find it easier to recall peripheral details – the colour, the binding, the typeface, the table at the library where we sat while studying it – than the content on which we were concentrating. If we think of a lecture we listened to with great concentration, we will recall the lecturer’s appearance and mannerisms, our place in the auditorium, the failure of the air-conditioning, much more easily than the ideas we went to learn. Even if these peripheral details are a bit elusive, they come back readily in hypnosis or when we relive the event imaginatively, as in psychodrama. The details of the content of the lecture, on the other hand, seem to have gone forever.

This phenomenon can be partly attributed to the common counterproductive approach to study (making extreme efforts to memorise, tensing muscles, inducing fatigue), but it also simply reflects the way the brain functions. Lozanov therefore made indirect instruction (suggestion) central to his teaching system. In suggestopedia, as he called his method, consciousness is shifted away from the curriculum to focus on something peripheral. The curriculum then becomes peripheral and is dealt with by the reserve capacity of the brain.

The suggestopedic approach to foreign language learning provides a good illustration. In its most recent variant (1980), it consists of the reading of vocabulary and text while the class is listening to music. The first session is in two parts. In the first part, the music is classical (Mozart, Beethoven, Brahms) and the teacher reads the text slowly and solemnly, with attention to the dynamics of the music. The students follow the text in their books. This is followed by several minutes of silence. In the second part, they listen to baroque music (Bach, Corelli, Handel) while the teacher reads the text in a normal speaking voice. During this time they have their books closed. During the whole of this session, their attention is passive; they listen to the music but make no attempt to learn the material.

Beforehand, the students have been carefully prepared for the language learning experience. Through meeting with the staff and satisfied students they develop the expectation that learning will be easy and pleasant and that they will successfully learn several hundred words of the foreign language during the class. In a preliminary talk, the teacher introduces them to the material to be covered, but does not ‘teach’ it. Likewise, the students are instructed not to try to learn it during this introduction.

Some hours after the two-part session, there is a follow-up class at which the students are stimulated to recall the material presented. Once again the approach is indirect. The students do not focus their attention on trying to remember the vocabulary, but focus on using the language to communicate (e.g. through games or improvised dramatisations). Such methods are not unusual in language teaching. What is distinctive in the suggestopedic method is that they are devoted entirely to assisting recall. The ‘learning’ of the material is assumed to be automatic and effortless, accomplished while listening to music. The teacher’s task is to assist the students to apply what they have learned paraconsciously, and in doing so to make it easily accessible to consciousness. Another difference from conventional teaching is the evidence that students can regularly learn 1000 new words of a foreign language during a suggestopedic session, as well as learn grammar and idiom.

Lozanov experimented with teaching by direct suggestion during sleep, hypnosis and trance states, but found such procedures unnecessary. Hypnosis, yoga, Silva mind-control, religious ceremonies and faith healing are all associated with successful suggestion, but none of their techniques seem to be essential to it. Such rituals may be seen as placebos. Lozanov acknowledges that the ritual surrounding suggestion in his own system is also a placebo, but maintains that without such a placebo people are unable or afraid to tap the reserve capacity of their brains. Like any placebo, it must be dispensed with authority to be effective. Just as a doctor calls on the full power of autocratic suggestion by insisting that the patient take precisely this white capsule precisely three times a day before meals, Lozanov is categorical in insisting that the suggestopedic session be conducted exactly in the manner designated, by trained and accredited suggestopedic teachers.

While suggestopedia has gained some notoriety through success in the teaching of modern languages, few teachers are able to emulate the spectacular results of Lozanov and his associates. We can, perhaps, attribute mediocre results to an inadequate placebo effect. The students have not developed the appropriate mind set. They are often not motivated to learn through this method. They do not have enough ‘faith’. They do not see it as ‘real teaching’, especially as it does not seem to involve the ‘work’ they have learned to believe is essential to learning.

answerEvidence.evidence: Educating Psyche by Bernie Neville is a book which looks at radical new approaches to learning
answerEvidence.reason: ‘Radical new approaches’ directly supports non-traditional ways of learning.

distractors.A: Suggestion is one theory discussed in the book, not the book’s main overall concern.
distractors.B: The introduction describes several radical approaches and several mental processes, not one emotion-based technique.
distractors.C: The book discusses effects of emotion, imagination and the unconscious on learning; it does not say emotion acts on imagination and the unconscious.

answerEvidence.evidence: we often remember what we have perceived peripherally, long after we have forgotten what we set out to learn
answerEvidence.reason: Peripheral details are incidental or unimportant details, and the examples show that they are recalled more easily.

distractors.B: The passage contrasts durable unconscious processing with conscious concentration and does not say hard concentration produces the best recall.
distractors.C: The consciously studied content is forgotten more readily than peripheral details.
distractors.D: The text discusses peripheral details and processing, not the importance of peripheral vision.

answerEvidence.evidence: If we think of a book ... we will find it easier to recall peripheral details ... than the content ... If we think of a lecture ... [we recall peripheral details] much more easily than the ideas we went to learn.
answerEvidence.reason: The two familiar examples are experiential support for Lozanov’s theory about unconscious and peripheral learning.

distractors.A: The examples concern what is remembered, not how concentration is developed.
distractors.C: Book and lecture examples produce the same contrast; the passage does not rank reading above listening.
distractors.D: Hypnosis is mentioned only as one way elusive peripheral details may return; it is not the point established by both examples.

answerEvidence.evidence: consciousness is shifted away from the curriculum to focus on something peripheral
answerEvidence.reason: Students’ conscious attention is deliberately directed to something other than curriculum content.

distractors.A: The method shifts attention away from curriculum details instead of asking students to memorise them.
distractors.B: Lozanov designs the indirect instruction; students are not told to invent their own instructions.
distractors.D: Reserve brain capacity is used, but teachers are not told to train students to avoid overloading it.

answerEvidence.evidence: In the first part, the music is classical ... the teacher reads the text slowly and solemnly ... The students follow the text in their books ... In the second part, they listen to baroque music ... the teacher reads the text in a normal speaking voice ... they have their books closed.
answerEvidence.reason: Several variables change: type of music, reading style, and whether students’ books are open.

distractors.TRUE: Contradicted by the multiple explicit changes between the two parts.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: The variables are described in detail, so the information is given.

answerEvidence.evidence: they develop the expectation that learning will be easy and pleasant

distractors.TRUE: The preparation creates the opposite expectation.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: The students’ expected experience is explicitly stated.

answerEvidence.evidence: using the language to communicate (e.g. through games or improvised dramatisations). Such methods are not unusual in language teaching.
answerEvidence.reason: The follow-up activities are explicitly described as methods that are not unusual in ordinary language teaching.

distractors.FALSE: The passage says the methods themselves are not unusual; only their exclusive purpose of assisting recall is distinctive.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: The comparison with ordinary language teaching is explicit.

answerEvidence.evidence: The paragraph discusses indirect recall activities and vocabulary learning but never states that students notice an improvement in their memory.
answerEvidence.reason: Neither student awareness nor a noticed general memory improvement is reported.

distractors.TRUE: Improved recall within the method does not establish that students notice a memory improvement as an indirect benefit.
distractors.FALSE: The passage does not say students fail to notice such an improvement either.

answerEvidence.evidence: few teachers are able to emulate the spectacular results of Lozanov and his associates
answerEvidence.reason: Teacher performance is discussed, but no teacher preference between suggestopedia and traditional teaching is reported.

distractors.TRUE: No statement says teachers prefer suggestopedia.
distractors.FALSE: No statement says teachers prefer traditional approaches either.

answerEvidence.evidence: Another difference from conventional teaching is the evidence that students can regularly learn 1000 new words of a foreign language during a suggestopedic session
answerEvidence.reason: The explicitly stated difference from conventional teaching is the much greater vocabulary learning achieved in suggestopedia.

distractors.FALSE: The passage presents the high vocabulary total as a difference from conventional teaching, not as inferior retention.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: A direct comparison with conventional teaching is supplied.

answerEvidence.evidence: Lozanov acknowledges that the ritual surrounding suggestion in his own system is also a placebo
answerEvidence.reason: The necessary element surrounding the suggestion is a ritual.

distractors.A: ‘Spectacular’ is an adjective and later describes results, not an amount of something necessary.
distractors.B: Teaching is the overall activity, not the element Lozanov says is needed to convince students.
distractors.C: ‘Lesson’ is a count noun and is not identified as the necessary surrounding element.
distractors.D: ‘Authoritarian’ is an adjective and cannot follow ‘an amount of’ here.
distractors.E: ‘Unpopular’ is an adjective and has no support in this sentence.
distractors.G: ‘Unspectacular’ is an adjective and later characterises other teachers’ results.
distractors.H: The ritual is described as a placebo, but the ‘amount of’ blank names the ritual itself.
distractors.I: ‘Involved’ is an adjective and does not name the necessary element.
distractors.J: ‘Appropriate’ is an adjective and later modifies ‘mind set’ in the passage.
distractors.K: ‘Well known’ is adjectival and concerns the method’s reputation, not what is needed to convince students.

answerEvidence.evidence: the ritual surrounding suggestion in his own system is also a placebo
answerEvidence.reason: Lozanov admits that the convincing ritual may merely be a placebo.

distractors.A: ‘Spectacular’ is an adjective and cannot follow ‘a’ as the required noun.
distractors.B: The ritual is not called a teaching.
distractors.C: It is not described as merely a lesson.
distractors.D: ‘Authoritarian’ is adjectival; the passage separately mentions autocratic suggestion.
distractors.F: The preceding blank names the ritual; the text then classifies that ritual as a placebo.
distractors.G: ‘Unspectacular’ is adjectival and refers to results, not the ritual.
distractors.I: ‘Involved’ is adjectival and does not fit the noun slot.
distractors.J: ‘Appropriate’ is adjectival and does not fit after the article ‘a’ without a noun.
distractors.K: ‘Well known’ is adjectival and describes reputation, not the nature of the ritual.

answerEvidence.evidence: suggestopedia has gained some notoriety through success in the teaching of modern languages
answerEvidence.reason: ‘Gained some notoriety’ is paraphrased by ‘has become quite well known’.

distractors.A: The spectacular description belongs to Lozanov’s results, not directly to the method’s degree of fame.
distractors.B: ‘Teaching’ is a noun and does not fit after ‘has become quite’.
distractors.C: ‘Lesson’ is a noun and does not describe the method’s reputation.
distractors.D: The text mentions autocratic suggestion but does not say the method became authoritarian.
distractors.E: Notoriety here establishes fame; the passage does not state that the method became unpopular.
distractors.F: ‘Ritual’ is a noun and names a component of the system, not its reputation.
distractors.G: ‘Unspectacular’ describes the mediocre results of imitators, not how well known the method is.
distractors.H: ‘Placebo’ is a noun and describes the ritual effect, not reputation.
distractors.I: The method is not said to have become involved.
distractors.J: ‘Appropriate’ modifies ‘mind set’ later; the method is not said to have become appropriate.

answerEvidence.evidence: few teachers are able to emulate the spectacular results of Lozanov and his associates. We can, perhaps, attribute mediocre results to an inadequate placebo effect.
answerEvidence.reason: Other teachers’ results are ‘mediocre’, hence unspectacular.

distractors.A: ‘Spectacular’ describes Lozanov’s results, whereas most other teachers fail to emulate them.
distractors.B: ‘Teaching’ is a noun and cannot characterise results after ‘have been’ in this context.
distractors.C: ‘Lesson’ is a noun and is neither grammatical nor supported.
distractors.D: Results cannot be described as authoritarian here; authority concerns how the placebo is dispensed.
distractors.E: The passage says the results are mediocre, not unpopular.
distractors.F: ‘Ritual’ names part of the method and cannot describe the results.
distractors.H: The placebo is an explanatory mechanism, not a description of the results.
distractors.J: ‘Appropriate’ modifies the desired mind set, not the quality of results.
distractors.K: ‘Well known’ describes the method’s notoriety, not most teachers’ results.

blindAudit.method: After drafting, physical pages 30–33 and 157 were reread independently in visual strips, with physical pages 29 and 34 rechecked for boundaries. The draft was checked against the page images for paragraph joins, sentence endpoints, punctuation, italics, question wording, option labels, answer sequence, and semantic-image need.
findings: The initial draft assigned the complete cross-page sentence beginning ‘Through meeting with the staff’ to raw page 30. The physical page break was corrected so raw page 30 ends with ‘successfully learn’ and raw page 31 starts with ‘several hundred words’. The canonical paragraph and sentence arrays were already complete and unchanged.

selfCheck.sentenceReconstruction: Each paragraph is exactly reconstructable by joining its mapped sentence slice with one space.
